### 2026-10-22 — DMA execution gate found; corrected boot reaches loading

The earlier zero-frame D3D initialization spin was a diagnostic launch omission. `RECOMP_PB_WALK=dma` selects the DMA-order parser, but the parser returns without consuming work unless `RECOMP_PB_EXEC` (or a scan-only diagnostic) is also enabled. With execution disabled, the guest's `D3DDevice` loop compared USER DMA PUT `0x80004000` with GET `0`, so the first D3D frame never completed. The corrected run set `RECOMP_PB_EXEC=1`; its first samples showed the GET catch up to PUT, and frame sequence advanced to `0x3AC` by 45 seconds. This corrects the launch configuration; it does not change runtime code.

A 420-second corrected x64 Release replay used `RECOMP_TRACE_BUDGET=0`, asynchronous I/O, APU/AC97 readiness and DSP acknowledgement, vblank/title events, the DMA walker and executor, the Steel Battalion USB profile, and the recorded timed input sequence. The framebuffer visibly reached pilot-name entry, birth-date confirmation, and `NOW LOADING`. At the watchdog it still showed `NOW LOADING`, so mission entry remains unverified. The final sample was in guest `D3DDevice_Swap` (`0x0020E5C0`), with target fence `0x2674B`, semaphore `0x26745`, device counter `0x26753`, USER PUT `0x00027F98`, GET `0x00023590`, and DCF4 signaled. The queue was being consumed but still had pending work; the loading stall or slowdown is not explained by the initial execution gate.

The same replay logged 27 DirectSound helper calls; every sampled release argument was valid object `0x01081004`. The earlier AV at `0xFE0001D4` did not recur in this run, which did not reach the same cleanup path, so audio ownership is not considered fixed. Audible output remains unverified. The initial comparison trace also confirmed the guest's initialization loop was waiting on USER DMA_GET to match DMA_PUT.

### 2026-10-22 — prior D3D swap/fence evidence

Two bounded x64 Release comparisons with the valid absolute live-input path reproduced a stop in `D3DDevice_Swap` (`0x0020E520`) calling `D3D_BlockOnTime` (`0x00211E10`). The guest waits on its title-created notification event at `0x0021DCF4` while waiting for pushbuffer/fence progress. With `RECOMP_TITLE_KEVENTS` disabled, the same guest loop receives `STATUS_UNSUCCESSFUL` and retries; this is not a usable workaround. With title events enabled, the host event is valid and is repeatedly set by the XBE graphics callback (software method 5). Ghidra 12.1.4's XboxDev XBE loader confirmed the callback at `0x00216EA0` signals the miniport event at offset `0x1A4`.

An 80-second low-noise run reached frame sequence `0x199` (409 swap frames) before the watchdog. The XBE's D3D callback routine `0x00216EA0` signals that event for callback code 5. This establishes that DCF4 (`0x0021DCF4`) is the D3D completion event in this wait path.

A serialized diagnostic x64 run reached pilot selection and held the presented frame at “List as New” through its 120-second watchdog. It ended in `D3D_BlockOnTime` waiting on DCF4; the matching callback had not signaled after the last wait sample. The NV2A USER queue still held about 21 KiB (`PUT=0x3EC94`, `GET=0x39F18`), with semaphore `0x1A3F` and device counter `0x1A43`. DCE4 was signaled repeatedly and was not the final blocking event. Since this run enabled `RECOMP_GUEST_LOCK=1`, its timing is diagnostic and cannot by itself establish default scheduler behavior.

A separate 45-second run without that guest lock profiled pushbuffer batches. It reached 111 flips (3.48 FPS for the sampled interval). Typical roughly 2.7 KB batches took 0.25–0.67 seconds; one scan spent 379 ms across eight method `0x17FC` draws on the CPU-raster path, while its four `0x1D70` semaphore releases took 0.002 ms total. At the watchdog snapshot, GET was 5,424 bytes behind PUT while the scan was executing. This directly identifies substantial CPU raster cost and queue lag in that capture. ### 2026-10-20 — upstream rasterizer research follow-up

Checked current XboxRecomp performance work against the local v0.13.1 renderer. Upstream PR [#228](https://github.com/sp00nznet/xboxrecomp/pull/228) has merged a worker-pool change that queues all triangles in one batch before dispatching rows to workers. The local `nv2a_pb_exec.c` already parallelizes each individual triangle, but it does not queue a batch's triangles together. Upstream reported a 5.5→about 15 FPS improvement on Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel; its test covers overlap order, which must remain stable for correct pixels. This is a relevant candidate for later gameplay rendering, not a verified Steel Battalion improvement.

Upstream PR [#231](https://github.com/sp00nznet/xboxrecomp/pull/231) proposes pipelining raster jobs behind pushbuffer decoding. It remains open and requires per-job copies of render state plus explicit drain points before synchronization and surface operations. The reported test was also Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel, with about 15.5→17.4 FPS; the author notes it had not been run on several other titles. It is not a safe drop-in change for the current Steel Battalion bring-up.

These two changes do not directly explain the measured 512×512 splash cost: that draw is only a pair of large triangles, so batching triangles would reduce worker handoffs but would not remove per-pixel combiner, blend, texture, and depth work. Do not import the open pipeline patch or claim either upstream result for Steel Battalion. Next, profile the current windowed build with the established boot flags and identify which exact splash fast-path gate or per-pixel operation accounts for the time; preserve the NV2A reference path for parity. No source was changed in this research check, no progress bar moved, and no title-screen/audio/gameplay status is revised.

This modest change does not resolve startup throughput and is not being made a default. That diagnostic was stopped after capturing enough samples. No runtime source change was made, and no game process remains.

### 2026-10-20 guest DMA wait and pushbuffer evidence

A 20-second watchdog run captured the guest at the same wait in `sub_00216010`: it compares the lower 28 bits of the USER DMA GET value at `0xFD800044` against `0x80004000` (the buffer base), while the runtime reports USER PUT=GET=`0x495C`. A local dump around the submitted segment tail (`0x8000491C`–`0x80004978`) contains no jump marker in those words. This narrows the problem to the difference between the title's expected return to the buffer base and the runtime's current “GET equals submitted PUT” acknowledgement; it does not yet establish the correct transition or prove this is the only boot blocker.

Checked upstream references before changing behavior: xemu's NV2A USER reads expose the PFIFO DMA_GET register, and its DMA pusher advances GET as it consumes command words and handles jump/call/return control flow ([xemu `user.c`](https://github.com/xemu-project/xemu/blob/master/hw/xbox/nv2a/user.c), [xemu `pfifo.c`](https://github.com/xemu-project/xemu/blob/master/hw/xbox/nv2a/pfifo.c)). nxdk's pushbuffer diagnostics also read the hardware DMA_GET register directly ([nxdk `pbkit.c`](https://github.com/XboxDev/nxdk/blob/master/lib/pbkit/pbkit.c)). No upstream code was copied. The current local worker still mirrors PUT to GET after its separate command scan, so faithful GET progression/control flow remains unimplemented. Temporary word-dump instrumentation was removed and the Release target rebuilt; no runtime source change remains. Milestone 3 and progress bars remain unchanged. Next model or trace the title's pushbuffer control flow and validate the wait transition, then rerun boot.

Imported a flat raw image of the user's XBE at image base `0x00010000`. Ghidra's focused auto-analysis completed successfully in 97 seconds. It independently identified instruction/function starts at `0x0002DB50`, `0x000DFF40`, `0x00211E10`, `0x0020DBC0`, `0x00216BE0`, and `0x00216EA0`, corroborating the existing function boundaries. Decompiled `0x000DFF40` calls `0x0002DB50(0x19)` (25 entries). `0x0002DB50` calls `0x0020EC60`, obtains the limit through `0x0020F2C0`, and waits in a predicate loop until `consumer + requested_count <= limit`. `0x00216BE0` has six call references and calls the XBE thunk at `0x0025D1E8`. This independently confirms the caller/request-size and callback path already under investigation; it does not explain why the runtime sometimes stops before the queue becomes available, nor justify a kernel/event change.

Keep this separate from the DCF4 queue-space wait: `0x00211E10` clears and waits on DCF4 when NV2A queue space is insufficient. The earlier title-reaching 120-second run's watchdog was waiting on DCF4 (`ESI=0x0021DCF4`, `ECX=0x0021B790`, USER `PUT=0x80F6C`, `GET=0x7C52C`). Correction: the `6` visible on the guest stack is the `WaitReason` argument to `KeWaitForSingleObject(event, 6, 1, 0, 0)`, not a six-entry request. Ghidra shows the actual queue-space helper compares the current pointer at `base+0x30`, the completion pointer at `base+0x34`, and the caller's target pointer; it also calls `0x00211AB0` to compute available space. The capture is not evidence that the DCE4 25-entry path stalled. The two helpers have different predicates, event words, and consumers; sample each against its own state.

Ghidra's optional Jython export script was unavailable, so the successful targeted report was generated with a local Java script. No decompiled game code, XBE, or asset was added to Git. Progress bars and Milestone 3 are unchanged.

### Queue-event mapping and bridge trace (2026-10-19)

Static inspection separates two adjacent guest events. The queue-space helper `sub_00211E10` waits on object `0x0021DCF4` (global object `0x0021B790` + `0x2564`), whose signal-state dword is `0x0021DCF8`. Its blocking call is at guest return site `0x00211F3B`; the helper first checks the NV2A ring-buffer producer/completion counters and waits when space is insufficient. The nearby event `0x0021DCE4` (`+0x2554`, signal state `0x0021DCE8`) is a separate notification event used by `sub_0020EC60`. Earlier traces that grouped them as one event were ambiguous and should be read with this distinction.

A temporary, opt-in bridge trace captured the queue wait at call `156010`: caller `0x00211F3B`, guest signal state `0`, host event result `WAIT_TIMEOUT` (258), notification type, then `WaitForSingleObjectEx`. No `KeSetEvent` for `0x0021DCF4` appeared before that wait. An all-event trace changed startup timing and logged repeated sets for the separate `0x0021DCE4` event from caller `0x00216CAE`; it did not establish the queue event's producer.

After restoring the bridge source byte-for-byte and forcing a normal rebuild, an uninstrumented 75-second run stopped at the same queue-event wait. External reads showed producer counter `0x529`, completion pointer `0x80003000`, queue-event state `0`, and separate title-event state `1`. The process memory reader could not read the completion word through the high alias, so the producer/completion gap remained unmeasured in that run. The watchdog saw NV2A `PUT=GET=0x7274C`; renderer logs counted 322 flips, 692 draws and 1,384 triangles, but no screenshot was collected for visual inspection. No title-screen, audio, input, or gameplay result is verified.

A follow-up used the runtime's own guest-memory sampler with the pushbuffer executor, packet scan, async I/O, modeled vblank, title event bridge, and synthetic AC'97 readiness enabled. The sampler read guest `0x80003000` as `0xAB`, while the producer at `0x0021B7C0` was `0xB7`; the gap was 12 entries against the helper's 8-entry threshold. The guest was still in `sub_00211E10` (`EAX=8`, `ECX=0xAB`, `EDX=0x80003000`, `ESI=0xB7`, `EDI=0x0C`), with NV2A `PUT=0x128A0`, `GET=0x11E08`. Semaphore logs independently show releases being written at host `0x80013000`, the mapped address for guest `0x80003000` with the run's `0x10000` memory offset. This establishes that the completion word is readable through the runtime mapping and that the queue was behind by 12; it does not explain why DMA stopped advancing or verify a visible screen. The event state was 1 at this watchdog sample, but the active wait was the queue fence, not a host event wait.

The normal Release executable was rebuilt with the original bridge SHA-256 `2190BBD3E20DA13238802F655F198ECEE5BCC8A123CF6A774142C298F47CF232`; the temporary `EVENTTRACE` marker is absent. Both follow-up diagnostic runs are complete, and no game process remains. Keep progress bars unchanged; Milestone 3 stays active.

### Pushbuffer GET-window inspection (2026-10-19)

A temporary watchdog-only dump captured the current GET window in a matched 90-second executor run. At the watchdog, USER `GET=0x12DEC`, `PUT=0x13DE8`; the first dword at GET was `0x00081D98`, an increasing packet for `SET_CLEAR_RECT_HORIZONTAL` and `SET_CLEAR_RECT_VERTICAL`, with full-screen bounds `0x027F0000` and `0x01DF0000`. The following words form ordinary NV097 clear/depth and state packets. An earlier sample at `GET=0x11E08` contained the same valid packet sequence, and the later sample had advanced to `0x12DEC`; this rules out a fixed malformed header at `0x11E08`.

The watchdog can observe a pending submission before the executor finishes it: the runtime updates USER GET to PUT only after `nv2a_pb_scan` executes the submitted segment. Thus a GET-window dump identifies the queue's last reported completion point, not necessarily the exact command executing on the worker thread. The same run reported 22 segments and 14,210 scanned words with no unrecognised words, 41 flips at 0.66 reported FPS, 80 vertex-program batches and about 24.6 million pixel writes. It had no textured batches in the measured summary and no visual capture; the low rate is a bring-up performance measurement, not an accurate gameplay benchmark.

The dump hook was removed immediately after collection, the normal Release target rebuilt successfully, and the test process ended at its watchdog. Logs and the GET-window sample remain local/ignored. Progress bars remain unchanged; Milestone 3 stays active.

A separate 60-second `RECOMP_PB_TIMING` run measured the latest submitted segment (`0x80005F40`–`0x800069D8`, 678 words). Method `0x17FC` (`SET_BEGIN_END`) accounted for 2,678.572 ms across eight packets; the next reported method total was below 1 ms. In the runtime, closing `SET_BEGIN_END` calls `draw_primitive` for these buffered batches, and the same report counted 12 vertex-program batches and 48 vertices. This localizes the largest measured cost to the CPU draw path, rather than to the clear-rectangle packet seen at GET. The 60-second run reached 19 flips at 0.53 reported FPS and ended at the watchdog; it did not verify the title screen, audio, input, or gameplay. These are bring-up measurements, not gameplay benchmarks.

Next: trace the `draw_primitive` program path and compare its CPU raster workload against an exact small reference scene before optimizing it; preserve framebuffer output and command ordering.

At 150 seconds, the watchdog found the guest waiting on event `0x0021DCF4`; NV2A `PUT=GET=0x62CD0`. The process exited and no runtime remains. This verifies a repeatable title presentation plus a scripted pulse after the visible prompt, but not game-side input acceptance, audio, or gameplay. No progress bars advance; Milestone 3 remains active.

### Latest bounded title and Steel Battalion USB input probe (2026-10-18)

A follow-up 180-second run kept the `RECOMP_PAD_LIVE` input file empty so no button was sent before the title prompt appeared. It stopped at the Dolby startup image and produced no new framebuffer captures after the first 44 seconds. The watchdog sampled guest stack pointer `0x00F7FE18`, registers `EAX=0x00F7FE60`, `ESI=0x80100080`, and NV2A USER `PUT=GET=0x645FC`; the process exited at its configured bound. This run neither reached the title nor tested game-side input. The stalled path is not yet explained.

A matched 120-second control with the same USB and graphics settings but no live-input watcher stopped at the same Dolby image. At timeout the guest snapshot again showed ESP `0x00F7FE18`; the queue had advanced to `PUT=0x38F88`, `GET=0x384F0`. This shows the watcher is not required for the startup stall. A second matched run with asynchronous-I/O mode disabled stopped on a black frame with `PUT=GET=0x495C`, so that toggle also did not recover startup. A temporary trace of the guest's repeated wait at return address `0x00191817` recorded a relative delay of `-660000` 100-nanosecond units (66 ms), confirming a normal polling sleep rather than an infinite wait. The temporary trace was removed and the ordinary Release executable rebuilt; no runtime is left running. These runs do not reach the title or verify audio/input.

An opt-in file trace confirmed that the guest opens handles with `CreateOptions=0x48` (asynchronous under the current runtime's classification) and issues `NtReadFile` requests of 133,120 bytes with no event or APC. The bridge completes the data read synchronously, writes the I/O status block, and returns `STATUS_PENDING` for those handles. Static XBE analysis shows the caller branches on `STATUS_PENDING` and calls `NtWaitForSingleObject` on the file handle. However, a targeted runtime trace did not capture that call at the expected guest call sites, so file-object wait behavior remains unverified and is not yet a confirmed cause of the Dolby stall. A later 120-second run still stopped at Dolby after reading `STRM00.WAV` through offset 262,144; its watchdog snapshot and framebuffer did not establish a deadlock. Temporary instrumentation was removed and the normal Release target rebuilt with no trace markers.

A combined 60-second run enabled both read and native-wait tracing. It observed asynchronous file opens, but neither the pending-read trace nor the low-level `NtWaitForSingleObject` trace fired. The guest continued sequential `READ` calls from `0x0018E95A` through `STRM00.WAV` and stopped at the same Dolby frame. This means the async-handle hypothesis from the separate trace was not reproduced in the actual stalled stream path; do not change file completion behavior based on it. All temporary hooks were removed and the ordinary Release executable rebuilt successfully.

Static disassembly confirms `0x0018E95A` is immediately after `NtReadFile` in a read/write stream-copy loop, distinct from the `0x0018E0AF` helper that branches on `STATUS_PENDING`. In the frozen-run log, the reader requested 65,536-byte chunks with no event/APC and each recorded call returned `STATUS_SUCCESS` with all 65,536 bytes. Successful-title and frozen-run logs both show reads at the initial offsets, but later bytes at matching offsets differ and the existing trace does not identify the handle/path or guest thread for each read. The title-reaching run enters heap cleanup after about 589,824 bytes, while the frozen run continues farther. The pending-file-wait theory therefore does not explain the observed successful reads. The next trace should include thread, handle/path, offset, and read/write status alongside frame/queue progress to establish where the runs diverge; no cause is confirmed.

A temporary thread/handle/path trace did not reach the filtered `0x0018E95A`/`0x0018E982` read/write calls. It logged the audio worker opening sequential `D:\Media\title\snk_*.sgt` and `.wav` assets, then the game crashed with `STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION` at guest VA `0xFFFFFFF4` in `sub_0021ED29`, called from `sub_0021FE7C` while walking an audio-object list under guest critical section `0x0023FE18`. A matched run after removing the trace hooks reproduced the same fault address and guest function, so the crash is not attributable to trace output.

A follow-up trace confirmed the values: startup caller `0x001108AF` entered wrapper `sub_00108CF0` with object `0x006C1E80`, whose first field was zero; the wrapper passed that zero as the object argument to `sub_00221B19`. That reached `sub_0021FE7C` with object and list head both zero, then attempted node zero minus `0x14`, producing `0xFFFFFFEC`; the callee's read at `[arg+8]` faulted at `0xFFFFFFF4`. XBE disassembly shows constructor `sub_00108420` initializes the first field of the object at `0x006C1E80` to zero. The bad list walk is confirmed, but the intended meaning of that field and why the startup path calls through it while null remain unverified. No behavior was patched. All temporary stream and generated-code trace hooks were removed, generated sources restored byte-for-byte from local backups, and Release x64 rebuilt successfully. Next: trace the guest code that should populate the `0x006C1E80` field and identify the expected audio object/list initialization sequence before changing behavior.

A 30-second bounded write-watch run reproduced the same access violation at `0xFFFFFFF4` in `sub_0021ED29`. The configured watch on the page containing `0x006C1E80` yielded no recorded value-changing write before the crash; because the run log does not preserve an arm marker or distinguish writes of zero, this is inconclusive about all writes to the field. It does not establish that initialization failed in this run: the captured log has no `DirectSoundCreate`/constructor HRESULT. Earlier traces did record `DSERR_NODRIVER` when the AC'97 ready status was absent, while other startup captures recorded successful constructor results, so initialization must be correlated with the crashing run before assigning the current crash to that failure mode. The XBE entry point and section map are documented; that is static analysis, not verified runtime behavior. The title-asset bar records a diagnostic read of the three title XPR files only, not complete filesystem compatibility. Pushbuffer handling records command processing and draw calls, not a correct rendered scene. A fresh local build completed and the XBE reached its entry point. An opt-in NV2A trace then observed display-mode setup and GPU semaphore releases before the process exited on an access violation in the XBE's audio cleanup path. It again recorded `DSERR_NODRIVER`, a null audio vtable, and invalid audio virtual calls. This corroborates the already traced failed-DirectSound cleanup path; it does not establish that the GPU caused the crash or that untraced startup now has deterministic behavior. With diagnostic AC'97 readiness and a fake DSP doorbell acknowledgement, the guest read additional resources and flipped three frames, but the captured output was black and the renderer found no usable textured batches. The fake acknowledgement clears commands without DSP computation, so this run does not verify DSP or audio behavior. The host DirectSound COM wrapper is a no-output stub and the generated game code uses its XBE-resident DirectSound implementation; neither is a verified audio path. The APU has a Windows XAudio2 output backend, but its GP/EP DSP is stubbed. The optional DSP56300 FFI bridge and its synthetic memory-map/lifecycle harness now compile in an isolated worktree, and the harness passes. The patch does not route GP/EP MMIO or execute DSP firmware, and it does not change the audio status bars. AC'97 readiness, DSP processing, safe audio cleanup, audible output, and a verified title screen remain unverified. These diagnostic hooks remain opt-in. The campaign bars remain at zero because no mission has been verified from loading through completion and progression.

#### Latest bounded rebuild and pixel trace (2026-10-17)

The isolated `RelWithDebInfo` game target rebuilt successfully with the installed Visual Studio CMake. A 15-second watchdog-bounded launch using the existing diagnostic AC'97-ready and fake DSP-ack options reached guest entry `0x00192C47`, read game resources, and produced a framebuffer capture. The capture was not a recognizable title screen; the trace still logged unusable texture batches and a mostly black output. Pixel tracing sampled the full-screen textured quad: texture samples and RGB output were nonzero, while diffuse alpha and final combiner alpha were zero. A vertex-program dump showed that the XBE's inline data supplied diffuse alpha `0` and its vertex program directly copied that attribute to the color output. With source-alpha blending enabled (`0x302/0x303`), the transparent quad correctly leaves the black destination unchanged. This rules out the current vertex interpreter inventing alpha zero for this draw, but it does not establish whether the game should advance to a later screen or change the submitted fade alpha. No renderer fix was applied. Diagnostic audio shortcuts remain in effect, so DSP execution and audible output are still unverified. No progress bars advance, and no title-screen or campaign compatibility is claimed.

#### Latest bounded DSP effects-image trace (2026-10-17)

The Windows target built successfully with a temporary local-only trace inside the translated DSOUND-section function. A watchdog-bounded launch read all 24,936 bytes of `Media\SndEff\DSSTDFX.BIN`; the function received the buffer and returned `S_OK`. Static tracing shows that the XBE-resident DSOUND path builds 32-byte mapping records, relocates GP-memory references, copies mapped image data, then writes and polls a command word. This identifies the guest-side transaction shape, but not the meaning of every record or whether the DSP accepted or processed it. A corrected 8-second launch observed GP scratch registers `GPSADDR=0x003C4000`/`GPSMAXSGE=206`, EP `EPSADDR=0x003DC000`/`EPSMAXSGE=19`, and nonzero frame-table registers. The actual GP/EP SGE tables and first mapped payload are in the `0x80000000` contiguous alias: a write watch caught the first GP entry and the watchdog sample showed a physical page address there. Earlier low-alias-only zero reads and addresses `0xFE832040`/`0xFE8320D4`, `0xFE852048`/`0xFE8520DC` were invalid. Synthetic AC'97 readiness and fake DSP doorbell acknowledgement were enabled, so `S_OK` does not verify DSP execution, effects, audible output, or the title screen. xemu's GP/EP reference uses the descriptor registers for scatter/gather DMA and bootstraps P memory on reset release. The project APU's physical resolver already selects the contiguous alias, but the DSP scratch/bootstrap callback is missing. xemu's 512-byte MCPX boot ROM is mapped in the CPU BIOS region and not passed to its APU initializer, so it is not established as DSP firmware. Next implement and synthesize-test the callback and reset bootstrap. Audio and all playable-feature bars remain unchanged.

**The latest verified state is not a playable game.** The title screen, graphics, sound, controller input, saves, cinematics, mission completion, and campaign progression remain unverified. We will report compatibility only after the complete campaign has been tested mission by mission.

### Prior bounded startup and DSP mapping check (2026-10-17)

The optional DSP56300 bridge aliases the GP/EP DSP memory descriptors to the ordinary guest RAM windows. A focused synthetic test passed for those aliases and their boundaries. With the pushbuffer executor enabled, the guest semaphore advances and both GP and EP reset-release transitions are visible. The next guest wait posts DSP commands at 0x803B8810; real firmware bootstrap and DSP cycles remain absent. The diagnostic fake ACK can advance file and GPU work but does not calculate DSP output. No recognizable Steel Battalion title screen, audio, controller, save, or campaign behavior is verified. The bounded process exited, and a subsequent check found no project game/emulator process active. At that checkpoint, the timer/event wait release and real DSP bootstrap remained unresolved. The later opt-in event/GPU check below verifies only the diagnostic wait release; real DSP firmware/cycles remain absent. Milestone 3 remains active.

### Latest opt-in event and GPU executor check (2026-10-17)

The title-built event wait returned success and advanced its guest signal/counter state under the opt-in event bridge. A separate 45-second watchdog-bounded run continued consuming NV2A commands through GET `0x9ED0` while PUT reached `0xA968`, counting 28 vertex-program batches and 56 triangles. It did not produce a recognizable Steel Battalion title screen. That earlier run reported degenerate coordinates and no usable textured batches; a later first-frame trace refines this finding below. The event/vblank paths and AC'97/DSP shortcuts were diagnostic only; default synchronization, real DSP/audio, correct rendering, input, and campaign remain unverified. The specific opt-in wait-release diagnostic bar is now 1/1; all playable-feature and default-compatibility bars remain unchanged.

### Vertex and complete startup-frame trace (2026-10-17)

A later bounded trace of the first startup frame refined the earlier GPU diagnosis. Its immediate-mode vertices form a 640×480 full-screen quad. The passthrough vertex program outputs those same corners, and the textured draw has UVs spanning `(0,0)` to `(1,1)` with a valid 512×512 DXT texture. The frame records two draws and four rasterized triangles; an earlier periodic capture shows only a dim CAPCOM logo. Thus the earlier degenerate-coordinate/no-texture summary does not describe this first traced startup frame. The image is still not the Steel Battalion title screen, and the dim appearance's cause is not established. No renderer changes or feature progress-bar increments were made. Separate 25-second vertex-input and 20-second full-frame traces exited at their guest watchdogs; a process check found no project game runtime active. Synthetic AC'97 readiness and fake DSP acknowledgement remain in use, so neither DSP execution nor audible output is verified.

A subsequent pixel trace sampled the texture and combiner output at two logo coordinates. RGB was about `0.28` and `0.61`, but alpha was zero at both points because the guest supplied diffuse alpha zero. With source-alpha / one-minus-source-alpha blending, the textured draw leaves the destination unchanged at those pixels. The local combiner's signed-identity mapping and final-combiner expression match [xemu's reference shader generator](https://github.com/xemu-project/xemu/blob/master/hw/xbox/nv2a/pgraph/glsl/psh.c), so this does not establish a combiner bug. Six flip captures progress from black to a dim CAPCOM logo: the first three are black, then the logo brightness grows across three samples. This suggests a guest-driven intro fade, but it has not been compared with an Xbox reference capture. The responsible draw/surface is not yet identified. No rendering changes or progress-bar increments were made; next compare surface and draw transitions across flips.

To inspect later logo draws, the opt-in vertex trace limit was increased to eight batches in the local XboxRecomp checkout and the Windows target rebuilt successfully (existing MSVC warnings remain). In a 25-second watchdog-bounded run, guest-provided diffuse RGB stayed at `0.690196` while alpha rose from `0` in batches 2 and 4 to `0.0470588` in batch 6 and `0.0980392` in batch 8; intervening batches were black/opaque. This is consistent with a guest-driven logo fade and argues against forcing combiner/blend output. It is not verified against Xbox hardware and does not reach the Steel Battalion title screen. No feature bars advance. Diagnostic AC'97 and DSP shortcuts remain active, leaving real audio unverified. Next inspect guest timer/event execution after the CAPCOM intro and the real DSP initialization path.

### Latest Milestone 3 startup trace (2026-10-17)

An 8-second watchdog-bounded launch exited with code 3. The guest call path reaches translated `sub_00211E10`, whose code polls for free space in a ring buffer at guest `0x00211F10`; the buffer's consumer and the reason it does not advance are still unknown. A separate lock trace observed worker thread 40308 waiting on guest critical section `0x00F86F88` while thread 32904 held and repeatedly released/reacquired it. The capture did not show whether the worker later acquired the lock, so starvation and causality remain unverified. Another diagnostic trace showed the guest timer advancing in 0.05 increments and finite 30 ms waits returning `STATUS_TIMEOUT`. The test used synthetic AC'97/DSP acknowledgements; it does not verify real audio. The Steel Battalion title screen and all gameplay features remain unverified, and no progress bar advances. Next identify the ring-buffer consumer and correlate it with the lock contention before changing runtime behavior.

### Follow-up: semaphore release advances startup (2026-10-17)

With the opt-in pushbuffer executor enabled, the trace observed NV2A semaphore releases of 5, 7, and 9 to guest word `0x80003000`; the watchdog sampled value 9 and the guest queue cursor at 11. NV2A GET and PUT both reached `0x495C`. The guest then reached a timed `KeDelayExecutionThread` call at the 8-second sample. This refines the previous ring-buffer observation: that polling came from a diagnostic run with pushbuffer execution disabled and is not established as a separate runtime defect. This run still used fake DSP acknowledgement and AC'97 readiness, and did not verify the title screen, real DSP execution, or audio. Progress bars remain unchanged.

### DSP scratch-to-P bootstrap verified (2026-10-18)

Implemented a bounded 0x800-word reset bootstrap using the corrected SGE registers and the guest's `0x80000000` contiguous alias. The focused Windows x64 harness passed across a two-page table, confirmed 24-bit masking and boundary copying, and rejected an incomplete SGE table. The full `your_game_recomp` target built with the optional DSP56300 FFI enabled. ### Bounded GP/EP execution scaffold (2026-10-18)

The XboxRecomp-specific bridge maps the DSP peripheral-status region through callbacks, keeps program-bootstrap readiness separate from the architectural interrupt bits, and schedules a 1,000-cycle FFI run for GP each APU frame and EP every eight frames. The JIT can consume whole translated blocks, so this value is a run budget rather than a strict maximum. Synthetic Windows x64 coverage verifies GP/EP status reads and clears, DMA-register round-tripping, scratch bootstrap, and bounded loop execution. The harness, APU library, and full game target build. The first corrected startup attempt exposed a stale generated dispatcher: five valid functions present in the refreshed XBE analysis were absent from the output. Regenerating the current 9,148-function translation added those entries with zero translation failures. A follow-up found the DSP reader was rejecting the guest's contiguous alias because it compared a 2 GB alias offset against the 64 MB physical RAM size; the resolver now validates the physical page against the contiguous allocation and reads the alias. A rebuilt 15-second launch, with pushbuffer execution and synthetic AC'97 readiness but without fake `RECOMP_APU_DSP_ACK`, loaded and executed the real guest GP/EP programs. It had zero unresolved indirect-call failures and reached one NV2A surface clear; USER DMA PUT/GET were both `0x495C`. The watchdog exited with code 3 while the guest polled command word `0x803B8810`; GPU diagnostics reported 235 unhandled methods. No verified Steel Battalion title screen appeared. This verifies guest-loaded DSP instruction execution only; DMA/control behavior, command completion, usable output, audible sound, title screen, and campaign remain unverified. The optional FFI remains disabled by default. Synthetic bridge, full build, alias resolution, and bounded guest-DSP execution are verified; player-facing audio stays unverified.

### Vertex DMA context gap (2026-10-18)

A 45-second externally bounded startup trace enabled complete pushbuffer-method accounting and vertex input diagnostics; it used the diagnostic pushbuffer executor, async file I/O, synthetic AC'97 readiness, and no DSP acknowledgement shim. It exited by external termination at the 45-second limit, with no game process left running. The log is local and ignored at `iso/local-analysis/logs/m3-vertex-dma-trace-20261018/stderr.log`.

The game's pushbuffer sets `NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_VERTEX_A` (`0x019C`) twice and `NV097_SET_CONTEXT_DMA_VERTEX_B` (`0x01A0`) once, each with handle `3`. The partial executor currently reports both methods as unhandled and does not retain those context handles. The upstream NV2A implementation stores these handles, then maps each vertex-array offset through the selected vertex DMA object; it also treats the high offset bit as the A/B selector ([upstream source](https://github.com/xqemu/xqemu/blob/master/hw/xbox/nv2a/nv2a_pgraph.c)). The four observed batches in this Steel Battalion trace are immediate-mode vertex submissions, so this missing array-DMA path does not explain the black framebuffer captured in those batches. It is a separate compatibility gap that could affect later non-inline geometry. No renderer semantics or progress bars changed.

Next inspect handle `3` in the game's RAMHT/PRAMIN state and compare its DMA descriptor with the pushbuffer offsets before implementing a bounded, generic vertex-array mapping. Keep the current black-frame diagnosis separate until another trace ties these vertex contexts to a failing draw. The run still did not verify a title screen, sound, or gameplay; Milestone 3 remains active.

### PMC interrupt enable gating (2026-10-18)


The original trace appeared to show a pending PCRTC hardware interrupt after its enable mask had become zero. A targeted assertion-time probe clarified the order: the hardware interrupt asserted with PMC pending `0x01000000` and enable `0x00000001`, then the guest ISR cleared the enable before the later status snapshot. The NV2A core's generic `pending && enabled` condition could also incorrectly allow a hardware interrupt under only the software enable bit, or vice versa. A small helper now gates hardware and software pending state with their corresponding PMC enable bits, following the [PMC register reference](https://envytools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/hw/bus/pmc.html). The standalone reproducibility patch is `patches/xboxrecomp-v0.13.1-pmc-irq-gating.patch`; its forward application was checked against the pinned xboxrecomp index. The separate host callback still carries the resulting IRQ line into the guest runtime.

The restored source had no obsolete trace print, but an incremental build initially left its string in the executable. I forced `nv2a_core.c` to recompile; the build output included that translation unit, the NV2A library and executable timestamps advanced, and a binary scan confirmed the marker was absent. A fresh 15-second bounded run then showed the guest NV2A IRQ being claimed, GP and EP DSP bootstrap plus execution slices, and title-media reads. The partial executor still reported 235 unhandled GPU methods, one surface clear, zero draw calls, and zero written pixels. The process was stopped at the external bound and its exit was confirmed. This verifies the refreshed binary and these startup paths only; no title screen, audible output, or gameplay was verified. Progress bars and Milestone 3 remain unchanged.

### Startup fade combiner interpretation corrected (2026-10-18)

The earlier pixel trace's zero alpha is consistent with the captured guest registers and does not by itself indicate a combiner bug. In the textured quad, the alpha inputs are `0xD4` and `0xD8` (V0.a and T0.a with signed-negate mapping); alpha output `0x000000C0` writes their AB product into R0.a. The guest supplies V0.a = 0, so this product is zero. The final-combiner G input `0x1C` reads R0.a, and the blend state is SRC_ALPHA / ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA. This matches the local evaluator and the corresponding behavior in [xemu's pixel-shader generator](https://github.com/xemu-project/xemu/blob/master/hw/xbox/nv2a/pgraph/glsl/psh.c); no rendering semantic change is justified by this trace.

Separate bounded captures show the guest later submitting the same logo quad with alpha rising from 0 to 12/255 and 25/255, alongside a gradually brighter CAPCOM image. That is consistent with a guest-driven fade, though there is no Xbox reference comparison. The latest 45-second no-ack trace still produced no recognizable Steel Battalion title screen; real DSP/audio, controls, and gameplay remain unverified. This supersedes the earlier hypothesis that the traced zero-alpha pixel itself demonstrated an unknown combiner/texture fault. No feature bars advance; Milestone 3 remains active. Next trace why guest startup remains at the CAPCOM sequence and correlate its event/timing and DSP state before changing renderer behavior.

### Vertex-program draw counters corrected (2026-10-18)

A fresh 60-second no-DSP-ack startup with the existing vertex-program dump and draw-verbose flags recorded two simple splash vertex programs: `oPos = v0`, `oD0 = v1`, and (for the textured pass) `oT0 = v2`. Therefore the earlier inference that the renderer received no usable screen coordinates is withdrawn. ### Steel Battalion XID protocol comparison (2026-10-18)

Static inspection of the embedded XPP helper `sub_00256F26` shows it builds interface control requests with `bmRequestType=0xC1`, `bRequest=1`, and `wValue=0x0200` and `0x0100` to retrieve output and input capabilities. Those values match the XID `GET_CAPABILITIES` requests documented by [XboxDevWiki's Xbox Input Devices reference](https://xboxdevwiki.net/Xbox_Input_Devices). That reference records the Steel Battalion XID type/subtype as `0x80/0x01`, with 26-byte input and 22-byte output reports; its interface uses Xbox class/subclass `0x58/0x42`, interrupt IN endpoint `0x82`, and interrupt OUT endpoint `0x01`.

The local virtual USB gamepad currently advertises a standard Xbox Controller-S XID profile instead (type/subtype `0x01/0x02`, 20-byte input and 6-byte output). This generic profile is not a Steel Battalion controller profile. The prior OHCI log contains no XID descriptor or `GET_CAPABILITIES` request, so the guest did not reach that part of device negotiation in the bounded sample; the cause remains unresolved. This is a concrete protocol gap, not proof that it caused the startup stall.

The community Windows driver [SteelBattalionDriver](https://github.com/caosdoar/SteelBattalionDriver) exposes the controller as USB-HID and is GPL-3.0. It is a reference for Windows device access, not a dependency selected for this project; no code was copied, and no project-wide license decision is implied. Next reproduce the guest's XID descriptor/capability negotiation in a bounded run, then compare any requests with this documented Steel Battalion profile before adding it to the virtual device. Do not claim controller input, output lights, title-screen boot, or gameplay from this static comparison. Progress bars remain unchanged and Milestone 3 remains active.

### 2026-10-18 follow-up: graphics-path wiring audit

The local runtime contains a Windows D3D8 COM compatibility layer backed by D3D11, and the umbrella `xboxrecomp` target links it. However, the observed title NV2A pushbuffer path is separate: `nv2a_pb_scan.c` decodes commands and, when `RECOMP_PB_EXEC` is enabled, dispatches them to `nv2a_pb_exec_method()` in `kernel/nv2a_pb_exec.c`, whose current visible-pixel path uses the CPU software rasterizer. The D3D8 bridge does not automatically receive this pushbuffer workload.

There is also an NV2A PGRAPH-to-D3D11 method translator in `src/nv2a/nv2a_pgraph_d3d11.c`. The current source documents it as a 5-dword inline-vertex, textured 2D menu profile; `pgraph_d3d11_init()` is called by the pushbuffer replay harness, while the normal scan path described above routes to the separate executor. A method-coverage audit is needed before judging whether this translator can be extended for Steel Battalion or whether a broader PGRAPH backend is required. Do not equate the existence of the D3D11 library with GPU-accelerated rendering of the game's current pushbuffer stream, and do not select or implement a replacement architecture yet. The exact `raster_batch()` timing above remains the measured performance evidence. Milestone 3 and all progress bars remain unchanged.

A source-to-trace comparison shows why the PGRAPH translator is not a drop-in renderer for the observed Steel Battalion startup workload. The 90-second guest run reported 52 vertex-program batches / 208 vertices with vertex attributes `v0` through `v15` in the observed attribute format. The executor also saw texture state at guest offset `0x803DF800` in 51 batches, but reported zero batches with a usable texture stage, so this is texture-state evidence rather than proof of successful texture sampling. The translator hardcodes five dwords per vertex (`X, Y, U, V, Color`) and its generic build path disables texturing and uses diffuse vertex color; a source search found no `GAME_HAS_FONT_ATLAS` definition in the local runtime checkout. Its optional texture mapping is a fixed reference-title lookup. The current executor separately interprets guest vertex programs and reports 155 distinct methods unhandled during startup; that count does not mean all 155 are visually significant. Any GPU path must preserve the game's vertex-program, texture, blend, and surface behavior, rather than forwarding this workload to the narrow menu translator. Next compare reuse options for the existing NV2A PGRAPH execution/shader code and define a semantics-preserving GPU raster backend; no backend switch or implementation is made by this audit.

### 2026-10-18 follow-up: renderer reuse and license boundary

The checked-out local XboxRecomp tree (`v0.13.1-dirty`) identifies the toolkit as MIT, with explicit LGPL-2.1-or-later exceptions for `src/apu/` and `src/nv2a/nv2a_regs.h`. Its contribution guidance specifically says not to port GPL code from Cxbx-Reloaded or the GPL portions of xemu. Cxbx-Reloaded publishes under GPL-2.0, and xemu's top-level `COPYING` is GPL version 2. Therefore, directly porting either project's PGRAPH renderer is not compatible with the current upstream contribution policy and would require a deliberate licensing review before any reuse. No code was copied and no project license was changed.

The viable research paths are to implement a semantics-preserving hardware raster backend against the existing decoded NV2A state using original code, or to pursue an explicitly approved GPL-compatible integration after reviewing project-wide distribution obligations and the XboxRecomp upstream policy. Continue with original-code feasibility and method-coverage analysis first; do not begin a GPL-derived port or change the license implicitly. Milestone 3 and all progress bars remain unchanged.

### Vulkan integration feasibility audit (2026-10-18)

Read-only inspection of xemu master `8fc3208` found 17 C translation units in `hw/xbox/nv2a/pgraph/vk/meson.build`; source files carry LGPL-2.1-or-later notices. Renderer functions are tightly coupled to xemu `NV2AState`/`PGRAPHState`, QEMU helper and memory-region APIs, shared xemu PGRAPH/surface/texture structures, and an offscreen GL context used for optional external-memory sharing.

The ignored XboxRecomp checkout has only a minimal PGRAPH state stub and a narrow D3D11 method handler. The Vulkan renderer cannot be linked in as-is. A port must map the real pushbuffer executor's guest state into a fuller NV2A/PGRAPH model or place the Vulkan renderer behind a new adapter contract, and must account for QEMU utility substitutions and the optional GL interop path. This is substantial engineering, not a hard dead end; it does not require the emulator CPU/kernel/machine loop. No source was copied, no build/test was run, and no milestone progress changed. The initial adapter seam is now documented: keep pushbuffer decoding and the current CPU VSH transform, send clipped geometry plus explicit render/surface/texture state to a Vulkan raster backend, preserve CPU raster as reference, and synchronize guest RAM only at true visibility boundaries. A read-only `vulkaninfo --summary` probe verified the installed loader sees the RTX 4070 SUPER (API 1.4.351, driver 617.42) and reports fragment-shader interlock, custom-border-color, external-memory-host, and dynamic-rendering extensions. No Vulkan SDK environment or development headers are configured. Next compare renderer extraction with a smaller Vulkan raster module, audit the exact build dependencies, and resolve a reproducible Windows Vulkan SDK/loader source without touching user ISO/game data.

### Logo wait loop identified as an NV2A semaphore wait (2026-10-18)

This is the producer of the exact word polled by `sub_00211E10`; the guest wait is tracking NV2A command completion. This rules out a missing kernel event as the immediate cause of the sampled wait. The executor does release the semaphore, but slow guest-visible progress remains consistent with the low software-renderer throughput and the narrow D3D12 coverage. It does not prove that rendering is the only limiting work.

### xemu shader-generator license boundary clarified (2026-10-18)

A pinned-source review found that xemu's Vulkan PGRAPH target is not solely an LGPL renderer path. The Vulkan shader cache generates vertex and pixel GLSL on cache misses; the called vertex-program generator and pixel/register-combiner generator carry GPL-2-or-3 notices and identify Cxbx/Dxbx/Xeon as prior sources. The Vulkan compiler wrapper also directly invokes glslang preprocessing, parsing, linking, and SPIR-V generation. These are required runtime paths in xemu's design, not unused files. See docs/VULKAN_REUSE_AUDIT.md for pinned source links and file-level findings.

Consequently, do not copy the complete xemu Vulkan renderer and describe it as LGPL-only. Before reuse, either clear a compatible project-wide/dependency license path, or replace the GPL shader-generation components with independently authored code and complete the remaining glslang/QEMU include audit. The existing project-owned CPU VSH and combiner implementations cite xemu behavior as reference; their provenance also needs review before distribution. No xemu code was copied or new runtime code added in this research update. The Vulkan backend remains locked, and no progress bars or Milestone 3 status change.

### NV2A nonzero NOP notification handling (2026-10-19)

A bounded 120-second profile recorded 263 nonzero payloads among the first 275 `NV097_NO_OPERATION` methods. The existing pushbuffer executor ignored this method, and the PGRAPH register handler treated interrupt status and enable registers as ordinary storage. The guest's ISR reads the PGRAPH trapped method and notification source; xemu's reference implementation models a nonzero NOP as a PGRAPH error/notification interrupt, records the trapped method/data, and waits for the guest to acknowledge it by writing the interrupt status register ([xemu PGRAPH implementation](https://github.com/xemu-project/xemu/blob/master/hw/xbox/nv2a/nv2a_pgraph.c#L2783-L2875), [xemu NOP notification method](https://github.com/xemu-project/xemu/blob/master/hw/xbox/nv2a/nv2a_pgraph.c#L3268-L3326)).

Implemented that device behavior in the local runtime and saved it as the isolated dependency patch `patches/xboxrecomp-v0.13.1-nv2a-nop-notification.patch`. The Release build succeeded. In a bounded profiled launch, NV2A traces showed the PGRAPH interrupt source asserted and the guest interrupt claimed it; the title art and “PRESS MAIN WEAPON BUTTON” prompt were visible. This verifies the notification/acknowledgement path can run through startup, not that the game is playable.

The same run ended at the 120-second watchdog in the separate queue-space wait on event `0x0021DCF4`, with guest `PUT=0x00080F6C` and `GET=0x0007C52C`. ### 2026-10-19 crash-site static follow-up

Mapped the keyboard-run crash's guest return address `0x00221331` against the local XBE translation and instruction listing. It returns into `sub_002212F4`, which calls `sub_0021E780`; the latter is a reference-count release helper that reads `[object+4]`, decrements it, and calls the object's first vtable method if the count reaches zero. ### 2026-10-20 kernel callback stack/register preservation

Compared the pinned XboxRecomp v0.13.1 runtime with the upstream callback fix ([commit 117a649](https://github.com/sp00nznet/xboxrecomp/commit/117a6498047c6ab93a48073875a071bff084c9a7)). The local `deliver_one_apc` called the guest completion routine and then advanced guest ESP by a fixed 12 bytes, even though the callback's stdcall return had already consumed its return address and arguments. ### 2026-10-20 — corrected DCF4 mapping and prompt-synchronized input pulse

Correction to the prior DCF4 note: `sub_0020EC60` does **not** wait on `0x0021DCF4`. The DCF4 waiter is in `sub_00211E10`: it clears `context + 0x2568` at guest instruction `0x00211E94` and waits on event `context + 0x2564` at `0x00211F39`, producing `0x0021DCF4`. ### 2026-10-21 — APU physical-page ownership resolves the voice-table overlap

Followed the upstream XboxRecomp APU resolver’s page-ownership approach after reading its current `apu_core.c` explanation: physical addresses can overlap ordinary XBE RAM and the separately backed contiguous-memory window, so address-range/high-water checks alone cannot identify the intended backing page. The upstream project is MIT-licensed; the APU implementation it incorporates retains its existing xemu LGPL notices. Reference: https://github.com/sp00nznet/xboxrecomp/blob/main/src/apu/apu_core.c.

A temporary allocation/voice trace proved Steel Battalion allocated contiguous memory at `0x80380000` for `0x8000` bytes, while voice 102’s table entry was at physical `0x00383300`, inside the XBE image address range. The old resolver selected ordinary image RAM. Added page ownership maps for allocated contiguous pages and pages explicitly named through `MmGetPhysicalAddress`; the APU now resolves named RAM first, then allocated contiguous pages, then the image and fallback ranges. The reusable change is isolated in `patches/xboxrecomp-v0.13.1-apu-physical-page-ownership.patch`; its reverse-apply check succeeds against the local pinned checkout.

Matched instrumented runs changed voice 102’s resolution from `0x00383300` to the contiguous alias `0x80383300`. Before the map fix, the voice list repeatedly remained at `0x0048` across 4,096 sampled idle events. With the map, the list contained `0x0066`, and only one idle event was sampled. This verifies the incorrect-page selection and corrected APU voice-table walk.

Removed all temporary trace code and rebuilt the Windows x64 Release target successfully. The clean 90-second launch produced the Steel Battalion “PRESS MAIN WEAPON BUTTON” prompt; its saved final frame is ignored under `iso/local-analysis/logs/m3-apu-physical-page-ownership-verified-20261021/`. The watchdog ended the diagnostic with its expected code 3, after the run slowed from about 13.8 FPS to about 1 FPS. No crash was logged. The mapping fix, rather than payload content, kept those writes out of the XPR alias.

### Upstream XboxRecomp investigation — DMA GET visibility
- Reviewed upstream XboxRecomp v0.16.0 (`f0f8a46`, released 2026-10-20) and its pushbuffer-walk change. It adds an opt-in DMA-accurate walk that publishes `DMA_GET` as commands are fetched. The upstream notes explain that XDK D3D reads GET during fence waits and may insert a software notification method when the GPU is behind; a GET value that only advances after a complete scan can therefore make it patch a command the executor already passed.
- This matches the shape of our delayed GET updates and outstanding-fence snapshots more closely than the earlier missing-event hypothesis. Our current runtime does handle nonzero `NV097_NO_OPERATION` through a synchronous PGRAPH notification, and DCF4 sets are verified, but delivery of the exact inserted notification during a progressing DMA walk is not yet proven.
- Upstream deliberately makes the DMA walk opt-in until a title's PGRAPH software-method interrupt path is confirmed. Do not replace the current scanner or make this behavior the default. Next add a bounded, opt-in comparison using the existing guest-safe runtime and capture GET, fence completion, DCF4, and title progress; keep a saved copy of the ignored local runtime source and retain the existing mode as the control.
- Reviewed [XboxDev/ghidra-xbe](https://github.com/XboxDev/ghidra-xbe) as an XBE loader and symbol-recovery aid. It is useful for further static analysis but is not needed to explain this runtime synchronization lead. No upstream source was copied, no dependency was installed, and the VS 2022 Build Tools already present are sufficient for the current target.
- Milestone 3 remains active; progress stays overall 2/8, decompilation 2/4, boot/compatibility 4/5, startup rendering 2/4, controller 2/3, and DSP/audio 1/2. Stable boot, audible output, full original-controller behavior, gameplay, save/load, and campaign completion remain unverified.

### XboxRecomp v0.16 DMA-walk comparison — notification works; stall remains
- The upstream v0.16.0 notes describe publishing NV2A DMA_GET while commands are fetched because XDK D3D fence code may insert a software wakeup command based on the visible GET position. This is documented in [XboxRecomp's upstream release notes](https://github.com/sp00nznet/xboxrecomp/releases/tag/v0.16.0). The upstream source is MIT licensed; the project's local prototype was adapted as a diagnostic and was not retained.
- Ran the opt-in walk for 70 seconds with the established title settings. It processed ring wraps and software notification methods and reached 719 flips at a sampled startup rate of 9.62 FPS. At watchdog, guest code waited on DCF4; USER PUT/GET were `0x4092C/0x3BF0C`, and the completion word/fence were `0xC57/0xC63` (12 behind). The queue was still outstanding, so this mode did not resolve the observed wait.
- A separate 45-second trace recorded at least 128 nonzero NV097 software notifications entering PGRAPH and all 128 returning after the guest acknowledged the interrupt. The trace also captured four DCF4 sets before the watchdog; DCF4 was signaled at the final sample. This verifies that the guest interrupt handler can service the notification path in this run. It does not prove that all notification placements, fence ordering, or timing are correct.
- A simpler packet-boundary GET experiment had shown a similar 12–14-count completion lag, so both experimental approaches were removed from the ignored local XboxRecomp checkout. The diagnostic notification logger was also removed. The ordinary XPP-seeded Release target rebuilt successfully afterward. No default runtime behavior was changed or committed; the original ISO and the user's unstaged XID patch were untouched. The bounded test processes exited and no `your_game_recomp` process remains.
- The new result narrows the investigation: event signaling and guest PGRAPH notification acknowledgement both occur, but the guest can still reach its DCF4 fence wait with an outstanding command backlog. Next inspect the exact command and semaphore-release ordering at the point the guest stops consuming; do not force-signal DCF4 or make the experimental walk a default. Milestone 3 remains active, with progress unchanged at overall 2/8, decompilation 2/4, boot/compatibility 4/5, startup rendering 2/4, controller 2/3, and DSP/audio 1/2.
- The repository already has a local Ghidra 12.1.4 distribution, and the public [XboxDev Ghidra XBE loader](https://github.com/XboxDev/ghidra-xbe) provides XBE format loading and XbSymbolDatabase recovery. It may help with a later function or import investigation. The extension was not installed, and no additional tools or dependencies were installed in this investigation.

### 2026-10-22 — DCF4 wait reviewed; corrected run advances into title-event wait

Static inspection of XPP guest routine `sub_00211E10` confirms the DCF4 wait is conditional. It clears DCF4 at `0x0021DCF4`, calls `sub_00211AB0`, and reaches the kernel wait only when that helper returns at least `0x2000`. A nonzero wait result repeats the wait; zero exits this helper to its caller. This does not establish what the caller does next or validate host event/GPU behavior.

The first correctly selected XPP-seeded replay omitted the previously established `RECOMP_VBLANK`, title-event, pushbuffer, async-I/O, AC'97-ready, and DSP-ack settings. It logged the untranslated `wbinvd` instruction and produced no tick trace; this was a misconfigured run, and there is no evidence `wbinvd` caused a stall. The two preceding DPC-seeded launches were also mismatched and are excluded.

This establishes how the bad value reaches the release helper, but not whether the selected virtual target, its calling contract, or a missing/incorrect thunk caused the invalid release. The [current XboxRecomp changelog](https://github.com/sp00nznet/xboxrecomp) records a v0.14 regression involving this-adjusting virtual-call thunks, later corrected for Half-Life 2. This is a useful pattern to compare, not proof that the pinned v0.13.1 base has the same defect; inspect this title's resolved target before considering a backport. ## 2026-10-22 — Ghidra identifies the DirectSound PIO FIFO wait

The older “GP sample counter” label for this address was incorrect; it is the VP PIO free-space register.

The experiment diff and captures are local/ignored under `iso/local-analysis/logs/m3-piofree-*`; no source change was committed. No game process remains, the original ISO and normal saves were untouched, and the user-edited XID patch remains unstaged.

### Follow-up — XBE worker entry and mission-mode flow recovered

Used the installed Ghidra 12.1.4 headless project to recover function boundaries missed by automatic analysis. The XBE thread trampoline at `0x001914F8` initializes per-thread TLS, invokes the callback pointer with its second argument, then calls `PsTerminateSystemThread` with the callback's return value. The callback at `0x00017E40` dispatches on game global `0x00347700`: mode 0 loads media streams and sound tables, mode 1 loads the selected texture range, and mode 2 runs mission initialization at `0x00034720`.

Mission initialization (`FUN_000F8690`) sets mode 0 during its own segment/cache setup, then loads the selected `segNN` XBE section. `FUN_00034720` runs the mission setup chain; the separate screen-update path uses `FUN_00101910` and related routines. The recorded `NOW LOADING` run shows a worker callback was created, but did not record the mode value or whether the callback completed. This does not establish that the worker, file cache, or graphics fence caused the stall.

No runtime or dependency behavior was changed and no new game run was started. Ghidra scripts/project and outputs remain local/ignored; the original ISO is untouched. The earlier `NOW LOADING` captures and pending graphics-fence evidence remain the strongest runtime observations.

### Follow-up — mode-2 worker scheduling narrowed

A second Ghidra xref pass recovered the mode writer `FUN_0001DAA0`. It stores the requested mode, waits for any prior worker to exit, and creates a thread using callback `0x00017E40`. The mission setup caller requests mode 2, raises that worker's priority, then suspends it; the main loop checks its exit code and resumes/suspends it around frame updates. Once the mode-2 callback returns, the displayed loading animation can continue while the main loop follows a different branch. This makes a screenshot alone insufficient to tell whether mission setup is still running.

The existing route log confirms creation of the callback thread but contains neither its mode nor its exit code. Next diagnostic should sample `0x00347700` and `0x00311BA4` together at the loading screen, plus the main-loop and NV2A fence counters. This is a more direct discriminator between a still-running mission worker and a completed worker with a stalled presentation/transition. No runtime behavior changed; no test was run.
